name: Light Node
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Traveling Light: Trusting the Chain Without Carrying It
lesson.summary: A light node keeps only block headers instead of the full chain, trading some independent verification power for a fraction of the storage and bandwidth a full node needs.
lesson.body:
Running a full node, as described in the Full Node chapter, means downloading and independently checking every block, header and body together, all the way back to the very first one. That is thorough, but it is heavy: it demands real disk space, real bandwidth, and real time before the node is caught up and useful. A light node takes a different bargain. Instead of downloading everything, it downloads only block headers, the small eighty byte summaries discussed in the Block Body chapter, and asks full nodes on the network for help whenever it needs more.

This works because of what a header can prove on its own. A header carries the previous block's hash, so a light node can still verify that the chain of headers is unbroken and that proof of work was spent on each one, exactly as a full node would. What a header cannot prove by itself is whether any particular transaction is actually inside the block it belongs to, or whether every rule in the system was followed by every transaction in that block's body. For that, a light node has to ask.

This is where the merkle root becomes useful again. A light node that wants to know whether a specific transaction was confirmed can ask a full node for a merkle proof: a short list of hashes that lets it recompute the merkle root from just that one transaction, without downloading the entire body. If the recomputed root matches the one already sitting in the header the light node already trusts, the transaction is proven to be included, at a tiny fraction of the data cost. This approach even has a name from Bitcoin's original design, simplified payment verification, since it verifies payment without doing the full validation work a complete node performs.

The tradeoff is real, and it is worth being honest about it. A light node is not independently checking that every transaction in the chain obeyed every consensus rule, the way a full node does. It is trusting that the network as a whole, and the full nodes it happens to be connected to, are enforcing those rules correctly, and it is leaning on the fact that producing a long chain of valid looking headers backed by real proof of work is expensive to fake. This is a meaningfully weaker guarantee than full validation, though it is still far stronger than trusting a single company's server.

In practice, this tradeoff is exactly why light nodes matter. A phone cannot reasonably store hundreds of gigabytes of blockchain history or stay online around the clock relaying blocks to peers. A light node lets a mobile wallet check its own balance and confirm its own payments by downloading a few hundred megabytes of headers and asking targeted questions of the full nodes it connects to, rather than the full body of every block ever produced. It is a deliberate compromise between convenience and the stronger trust model a full node offers, and most people interacting with a blockchain day to day are using a light node, whether they realize it or not.
